title: Those “Cafeteria Kids” Fighting Each Other in that Nikole Hannah-Jones Essay 25, 2026
author: Michael Goldstein
source: Center for Teen Flourishing musings: CTF WTF (michaelgoldstein.substack.com), September
summary: Michael Goldstein of the Center for Teen Flourishing shifts attention from Nikole Hannah-Jones's choices to the children she saw fighting unsupervised in her daughter's school cafeteria. After briefly recommending responses by Roland Fryer, Chris Stewart, and Andy Rotherham, he asks what it is like to give or receive those blows and who helps such children process them. The heart of the post is an interview with Emily Devlin, a former school social worker in a high-poverty Boston school who now works on Behavioral Activation at SocialRx. Devlin explains that much externalizing behavior is a trauma response to abuse, neglect, and unmet basic needs, and that the trust needed for disclosure can take years in a school setting constrained by the class schedule. The conversation ends with a proposed experiment on whether letting teens choose their own coach or clinician, even on vibes, improves outcomes.
points: Goldstein reframes the Hannah-Jones cafeteria scene around the experience of the children doing and receiving the hitting.
Devlin reports that fighting, running out of class, and chronic absence often reflected trauma rather than ADHD or anxiety.
School social workers frequently supplied food, housing help, and mattresses to address social determinants of health.
In schools, a child's disclosure of abuse can take years because the setting forces quick, contained sessions before returning to class.
Devlin strongly endorses testing whether giving teens a choice of helper, including paraprofessionals, improves results.
quotes: If you’re a CTF reader, I’m not only betting that you’ve read the essay in question, but setting the over/under for the number of NHJ essay responses that you’ve read at: 4.

But a lot of the time those externalizing symptoms weren’t really a symptom of that. They were a trauma response. These were kids dealing with abuse, neglect, social-determinants-of-health needs that made it hard to function.

Year three was often the hardest in a relationship, because that’s when a kid would finally say something they’d never told anyone - abuse, neglect - because by then I was a trusted person. But it took years.
Emily: Exactly, or in a hospital setting too. I think it’s because in a school setting, we’re trained, as professionals, to know: I’ve got to send this kid back to math in 20 minutes.
We can run every behavioral intervention in the world, but the reality is we’re in active crisis.
Emily: Agency and choice are the biggest thing, honestly, in any of this. Yes, unequivocally.
But it’s paired with another empirical finding, which is that paraprofessionals - for lack of a better word - are delivering roughly the same outcomes as credentialed clinicians.
